text: Encrypting data at rest only matters as much as the key management behind it. This lesson goes into the two services that actually hold those keys — Azure Key Vault and AWS KMS — because the access model each one uses, and how rotation really works, decides how much that encryption is actually protecting you.

Azure Key Vault stores three distinct object types. Keys are cryptographic keys used for encrypt and decrypt or sign and verify — this is what backs customer-managed-key encryption from the last lesson. Secrets are arbitrary blobs like connection strings, API keys, and passwords, stored as ciphertext and returned on request. Certificates are X.509 certificates, with Key Vault handling renewal through an integrated certificate authority.

Access to a vault works one of two ways, and both still show up in live environments. Vault access policies, the original model, are a flat list attached directly to the vault — vault-scoped only, invisible to a subscription-wide access review. Azure RBAC for Key Vault, the current recommendation, governs the vault's data plane through standard role assignments like Key Vault Secrets User, scoped the same way any other Azure RBAC role is. A vault runs one model or the other, so check which before assuming RBAC assignments are actually in control.

AWS KMS works differently from IAM alone. Every KMS key carries its own key policy — a resource-based policy attached directly to the key, separate from any IAM policy on a user or role. For a principal to use that key, both the IAM policy and the key policy have to allow it; it's an intersection, not an either-or. Most customer-managed keys ship with a default key policy that delegates control back to IAM, which is exactly why removing that statement can lock everyone out, with no IAM policy able to restore access without the account root user.

Rotation on either service generates new key material on a schedule — Key Vault's is configurable, KMS customer-managed keys rotate annually by default — but old versions stay available, so data encrypted previously remains decryptable. Rotating a key is never the same as re-encrypting everything under it. And getting a secret to an application works the same shape on both clouds: a managed identity on Azure, or an IAM role on AWS, lets the app authenticate as itself and fetch the secret at runtime, so nothing ever gets hardcoded into code or configuration.

Next lesson turns to what happens when storage access controls fail entirely — the public storage bucket problem — and the specific settings that actually prevent it, on both Azure Blob Storage and S3.
